## Study time depends on when space is available {#motivation}

- In this example, paid work and caring duties constrain study schedules.
- Evening capacity is limited, so not every applicant receives access.
- An eligibility threshold creates a possible local comparison.

  - The threshold is known in advance.
  - Its credibility depends on students' inability to manipulate their score.
  - Linked records follow course progress for four terms.

::: {.aside}
This is a fictional study. All observations, figures, and estimates are
synthetic; they illustrate the reasoning rather than establish an empirical finding.
:::

::: notes
Start with the student's scheduling constraint. Introduce the eligibility rule
only after the audience understands why evening access might matter.
:::

## Could evening access improve course progress? {#question-and-preview}

Does eligibility for evening access help students make progress?

::: {.incremental}
1. Access rises sharply at the eligibility threshold.
2. Course completion improves during the first two terms.
3. Subgroup estimates are larger for students with inflexible schedules.
:::

::: {.live-only}
> What would access change: study time, where students study, or both?
:::

::: {.handout-only}
Reading guide: distinguish the effect of eligibility, the effect of receiving
access, and the proposed study-time mechanism. They are different questions.
:::

::: notes
Invite two explanations before revealing the preview. Return to them after
the estimates: neither larger subgroup effects nor a positive average effect
identifies the mechanism by itself.
:::

# Setting and data

A SIMPLE RULE, A LINKED PANEL, AND A SHARP THRESHOLD

## A score of 60 determines eligibility {#access-rule}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%"}
- Applicants receive a priority score from 0 to 100.
- Evening access is offered when $s_i \geq 60$.
- Capacity and opening hours are fixed for the term.[^assignment]
:::
::: {.column width="68%"}
![](assets/threshold.svg){fig-alt="Synthetic evening-access rates jump at the eligibility threshold of sixty"}
:::
::::

[^assignment]: The fictional rule is deterministic within each application round.

## A room available after the working day {.full-bleed background-image="assets/field.svg" background-size="cover" background-alt="An illustrated university reading room at dusk" #study-space}

Reading rooms stay open until midnight during teaching terms.

The intervention changes access to a quiet room, not teaching or course content.

::: {.attribution}
Synthetic dusk scene · generated illustration, not a photograph
:::

# Research design

LOCAL COMPARISONS AROUND A PRE-ANNOUNCED ACCESS RULE

## Eligibility changes access; access may change progress {#assignment-pathway}

![](assets/pathways.svg){fig-alt="A pathway from priority score through evening access and study time to course progress"}

::: {.attribution}
Synthetic design diagram · arrows encode the estimand, not empirical findings
:::

::: notes
Read the upper arrows as the proposed causal chain. Schedule constraints
could modify the effect of access without being changed by eligibility.
:::

## An access effect also needs the first stage {#estimating-equations}

**First stage**

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{it} &= \pi_0 + \pi_1 \operatorname{Above}_{it}
  + f_-(r_{it}) + f_+(r_{it}) \\
&\quad + \lambda_t + u_{it}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Effect of receiving access**

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{it} &= \alpha + \beta \widehat{D}_{it}
  + g_-(r_{it}) + g_+(r_{it}) \\
&\quad + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{it}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The outcome jump measures eligibility's effect. Divide by the access jump
to recover $\beta$ under the identifying assumptions.

::: {.slide-nav}
[First stage: $\widehat{\pi}_1$](#first-stage)
:::

## The comparison needs continuity at the cutoff {#what-must-hold}

::: {.callout-note title="Estimand"}
$\beta$ is the local average effect of access for applicants whose take-up
changes with eligibility near $r_i = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Identifying assumption"}
Potential outcomes are continuous in the priority score at the threshold:
nothing but access changes discontinuously at $s_i = 60$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Caveat"}
Continuity is not testable directly; the diagnostics on the next slides probe
its observable implications.
:::

::: {.aside}
An interpretation as an effect of access also requires a relevant first
stage, monotonic take-up, and no direct effect of eligibility beyond access.
:::

## Eligibility raises access by 31 percentage points {#first-stage}

![](assets/threshold.svg){.r-stretch fig-alt="Synthetic regression discontinuity plot with a large access jump at the threshold"}

- Access increases by **31 percentage points** at the threshold.
- The jump supplies the first-stage variation; uncertainty must be checked separately.

::: {.slide-nav}
[Estimating equations](#estimating-equations){.back}
:::

## Fit separate trends within 12 score points {#specification-details}

- $r_{it} = s_{it} - 60$ is the centered score; $\operatorname{Above}_{it}=\mathbf{1}[r_{it}\geq0]$.
- Local linear fits are estimated separately on either side of the cutoff.

  - Preferred bandwidth: $|r_{it}|<12$.
  - Application-round fixed effects absorb common shocks.
  - Standard errors are clustered by student.

- The estimand is local to compliers: $\beta = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid r_i=0,\ \text{complier}]$.

EFFECTS, UNCERTAINTY, AND USEFUL ALTERNATIVES

## Eligibility raises completion by 0.18 courses {#main-effect}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
![](assets/estimate.svg){fig-alt="Synthetic main estimate with a confidence interval"}
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
- Point estimate: **0.18 courses per term**
- 95% interval: **0.07–0.29**
- Mean completion over the first two terms
- $N=4{,}087$ students
:::
:::

::: {.aside}
This is the effect of eligibility near the threshold, not the IV effect of
receiving access. Values and intervals are illustrative.
:::

::: notes
Pause on the interval before discussing magnitude. Explain that 0.18 is an
average across applicants, not a claim that each student completes the same
fraction of a course.
:::

## Nearby specifications give similar estimates {#robustness-summary}

| Specification | Estimate | Standard error | $N$ |
|:--------------|---------:|---------------:|----:|
| Baseline | [0.18]{.emph} | 0.06 | 4,087 |
| Narrow bandwidth | 0.20 | 0.08 | 2,744 |
| Donut specification | 0.17 | 0.07 | 3,801 |
| Covariate adjustment | 0.18 | 0.06 | 4,087 |

::: {.table-note}
Synthetic eligibility effects on courses completed per term. Standard errors
are clustered by student; bandwidth changes alter the estimation sample.
:::

::: {.slide-nav}
[Main result](#main-effect){.back}
[Placebo](#appendix-placebo)
[Alternative outcome](#appendix-alternative)
:::

## Inflexible schedules have the largest estimate {#heterogeneity}

| Subgroup, by baseline schedule flexibility | Estimate | Standard error | Share of sample |
|:-------------------------------------------|---------:|---------------:|----------------:|
| Inflexible schedule (work or care obligations) | [0.27]{.emph} | 0.09 | 31% |
| Partially flexible schedule | 0.16 | 0.07 | 42% |
| Fully flexible schedule | 0.09 | 0.08 | 27% |

::: {.table-note}
Eligibility effects come from the baseline specification interacted with the
schedule-flexibility indicator recorded at application; standard errors are
clustered by student. The table alone does not establish that subgroup effects
differ statistically or identify why they differ.
:::

## The eligibility effect is local {.dark-bg background-color="#1e293b" #design-identifies}

> A credible interpretation requires access to change sharply while other
> determinants of course progress remain smooth at the threshold.

::: {.incremental}
- The estimate is local to marginal applicants.
- It combines take-up, opening hours, and the option of a quiet room.
- It does not identify the effect of studying one additional hour.
:::

## Other institutions may see different effects {.light-bg background-color="#ffeac2" #scope-condition}

- The mock institution has scarce evening capacity and a transparent rule.
- Effects may differ when:

  - access is universal;
  - online resources are close substitutes; or
  - students can precisely manipulate assignment.

Return to the [identifying assumptions](#what-must-hold) before extending
the interpretation beyond this setting.

# Conclusion

WHAT THE SYNTHETIC EXERCISE WOULD SUPPORT

## Three takeaways {#three-takeaways}

1. A transparent threshold can support a credible local comparison.
2. Eligibility raises short-run course progress in the mock data.
3. Schedule constraints suggest a pathway that needs separate evidence.

::: {.callout-tip title="Result"}
In the synthetic example, eligibility raises completion by 0.18 courses per
term near the threshold over the first two terms. This is an offer effect.
:::

::: {.attribution}
After Hours · synthetic study · no empirical policy conclusion
:::

::: notes
Return to the opening constraint, then state the scope condition once.
:::

## Prepare the local comparison {#reproducible-specification}

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|3-5|6"}
sample <- subset(applicants, abs(priority_score - 60) < 12)
sample$centered_score <- sample$priority_score - 60
sample$above <- as.integer(sample$centered_score >= 0)
design <- model.matrix(~ above * centered_score, data = sample)
rounds <- factor(sample$application_round)
cluster <- sample$student_id
```

::: notes
This inert example prepares the design inputs only; no estimate or interval
is computed. Eligibility effects use the local outcome discontinuity. Access
effects require an instrumental-variables estimator and student-clustered
inference, not ordinary OLS standard errors from a regression on fitted treatment.
:::

::: {.slide-nav}
[Alternative outcome](#appendix-alternative){.back}
:::

## What a real study would still need {.light-bg background-color="#f1f5f9" #design-contract}

The synthetic exercise leaves empirical work to do:

- verify the assignment rule and actual take-up;
- assess score manipulation, covariate continuity, and missing outcomes;
- report first-stage strength, uncertainty, and sensitivity to bandwidth;
- distinguish access effects from mechanisms and subgroup differences;
- establish whether the local result is relevant to a broader policy.

::: {.attribution}
Synthetic example · assumptions require evidence
:::
